issues.legal_issue: A later amendment expanding revisional jurisdiction does not apply to a revision concerning an appellate decree that became final under the earlier law before the amendment.
material_facts: The eviction suits were filed before the amendment to the rent statute’s revisional provision.
The appellate court’s decrees became final under the provision as it stood before the amendment.
The revisions were heard after the amendment, and the High Court relied on the amended provision to review the appellate decisions.
issues.conclusion: The amended revisional provision could not be used to review the decrees; the High Court could consider the revisions only under its ordinary civil revisional jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: As held in Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas, an amendment made after an appellate decree has become final under the former Section 29(2) of the Bombay Rent Act cannot be used to set that decree aside. The amendment made by Gujarat Act 18 of 1965 did not govern these proceedings insofar as it purported to enlarge the High Court’s power over the already-final appellate decrees.

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision arising from an appellate decision in a rent-control case.
predicates.appellate_decision_final_before_procedur: The appellate decision became final under the earlier procedural law before a later amendment was enacted.
predicates.revision_considered_after_procedural_ame: The revision was considered after the later procedural amendment was enacted.

issues.definition: When a rent-control revision concerns an appellate decision that became final before a later procedural amendment, the amended review power is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A civil revisional court cannot interfere merely because a lower court may have construed the applicable law incorrectly when the lower court had jurisdiction and did not exercise it illegally or with material irregularity.
material_facts: Both the trial court and the appellate court had jurisdiction to decide which statutory rent category applied to the tenancies.
Both courts found that the cases fell within the same statutory category and ordered eviction.
The High Court disturbed those decisions after relying on the amended revisional provision, although the cases were reviewable only under ordinary civil revisional jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court considered that even if the lower courts’ construction of the relevant provisions was erroneous, that would not establish illegal or materially irregular exercise of jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts’ decisions could not be disturbed in civil revision on the basis of an allegedly erroneous construction of the statute alone. The High Court’s order was set aside and the appellate decrees were confirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an erroneous construction of a statute does not by itself amount to exercising jurisdiction illegally or with material irregularity. The Court relied on Batilal v. Ranchhodbhai and Abbasbhai v. Gulamnabi, both concerning the limits of revisional interference; it also noted that the courts below had jurisdiction to determine whether the cases fell under Section 12(3)(a) or Section 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rent Act.

predicates.civil_revision_from_appellate_decree: The proceeding is a civil revision arising from an appellate decree.
predicates.lower_courts_had_jurisdiction_to_decide_: The lower courts had jurisdiction to decide the legal classification at issue.
predicates.alleged_error_was_only_erroneous_legal_c: The asserted error was an incorrect construction of the law, without an independent showing of illegal or materially irregular exercise of jurisdiction.

issues.definition: If an appellate decree is challenged in civil revision, the lower courts had jurisdiction to decide the issue, and the alleged defect is only an erroneous legal construction, revisional interference is not justified.
